name: RP³ Geon
description: Schwarzschild's black hole with its second exterior folded onto the first: the Kruskal events $(T, X, \theta, \phi)$ and $(T, -X, \pi - \theta, \phi + \pi)$ are one event. Outside the horizon it is Schwarzschild's spacetime, and behind it the black hole and the white hole are each half of Kruskal's. Space at the moment of time symmetry is real projective space with a point removed, and the spacetime is orientable in time and in space.
convention: The Schwarzschild radius is $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, and we keep factors of $c$ explicit. An event is a pair of points of Kruskal's manifold, $(T, X, \theta, \phi)$ and $(T, -X, \pi - \theta, \phi + \pi)$. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: Schwarzschild's black hole, drawn in full, has two outsides [kruskal1960]. Martin Kruskal's coordinates of 1960 cover the whole of the solution, and beyond the horizon they show a second universe as large as the first, joined to ours for a moment by a throat of radius $r_s$ [kruskal1960, giulini2018]. The throat was already known as the bridge of Albert Einstein and Nathan Rosen, who in 1935 joined two sheets of space across it as a model of a particle [einstein1935]. It came back in 1957, when Charles Misner and John Wheeler set out to build mass and charge from empty curved space, "mass without mass" and "charge without charge" [misner1957]. Einstein and Rosen's picture, as they described it, needed "a mirror space, close to and parallel to the first space", and they looked for a space that does without it, one with a single region that flattens out far away [misner1957].¶Where does the throat lead? Misner and Wheeler's answer was that it could lead back to the side it starts from [misner1957]. In the isotropic radius $\rho$ the moment at which the throat is widest has the metric $$ds^2 = \left(1 + \frac{r_s}{4\rho}\right)^4\left(d\rho^2 + \rho^2d\Omega^2\right),$$ and the inversion $\rho \to r_s^2/16\rho$ swaps the two sheets and leaves every distance as it was [misner1957]. They followed the inversion with a trip to the opposite point of the sphere, $\theta \to \pi - \theta$ and $\phi \to \phi + \pi$, so that no point stays where it is, and declared each point the same as its image [misner1957]. The result is "a new manifold with only one region", and its space at that moment is "projective 3-space" with "one point removed", the point at infinity [misner1957]. Fall straight into the throat and you climb out of the same throat on its far side, in the universe you left [misner1957, giulini2018].¶Kruskal's coordinates, three years later, carry the fold to the whole spacetime [kruskal1960, giulini2018]. In them it is $(T, X, \theta, \phi) \to (T, -X, \pi - \theta, \phi + \pi)$: keep the right half of Kruskal's diagram, and glue its left edge $X = 0$ to itself across the sphere [louko1998, giulini2018]. One exterior is left, with a black hole in its future and a white hole in its past, and every point of the edge is a sphere with opposite points made one, a projective plane [friedman1993, giulini2018]. The name RP³ geon dates from 1993 and is due to John Friedman, Kristin Schleich, and Donald Witt [friedman1993]. Geon was Wheeler's word of 1955 for a body made of nothing but fields and their own gravity, and Rafael Sorkin widened it in 1985 to any space that is flat far away and has a topology other than that of ordinary space [wheeler1955, sorkin1986, louko2010]. By the count of Jorma Louko and Donald Marolf the spacetime is "inextendible, globally hyperbolic, space and time orientable", and in every small region it is Kruskal's [louko1998].¶The fold that reverses $T$ along with $X$ is another spacetime, the elliptic interpretation of the black hole that Gary Gibbons examined in 1986, which keeps the static symmetry of the exterior and gives up the difference between future and past [gibbons1986elliptic, louko1998, giulini2018]. The geon trades the other way: time keeps its direction, and the symmetry under shifts of Schwarzschild's $t$ holds only outside the horizon, since the fold reverses the Killing vector that generates it [louko1998, giulini2018]. Of the moments $t = $ const of the exterior, one alone continues smoothly behind the horizon into a slice of the whole spacetime [louko1998]. Which one it is cannot be read off outside: probing only the exterior, in Louko and Marolf's words, "provides no clue" [louko1998].¶Can anyone outside find the fold? Light sent in from far away crosses the horizon before it reaches the edge, and ends on the singularity [friedman1993]. This is topological censorship, the theorem Friedman, Schleich, and Witt proved in 1993 for every structure of this kind: "general relativity does not allow an observer to probe the topology of spacetime", since the structure "collapses too quickly to allow light to traverse it" [friedman1993]. An older theorem, Dennis Gannon's of 1975, says that a space with such a structure in it, flat far away and filled with nothing of negative energy, cannot evolve without a singularity [gannon1975, friedman1993]. Looking is still allowed: light that left the white hole reaches an observer outside by two routes, one direct and one through the fold, and the geon is their example of it [friedman1993].¶A black hole with one outside puts the Hawking temperature to a test [louko1998]. The standard arguments for it lean on Kruskal's two exteriors, each quantum of the radiation having a partner in the other universe [louko1998]. On the geon both partners live in the one exterior, and Louko and Marolf found in 1998 that the hole still "appears as a thermal bath with the standard Hawking temperature" to an observer far away at very early and very late times [louko1998]. Its entropy, counted by the path integral, came out as "only half of the Bekenstein-Hawking entropy" of Schwarzschild's hole of the same mass, the half that goes with the projective plane where the horizons cross, of area $2\pi r_s^2$ where Kruskal's sphere has $4\pi r_s^2$ [louko1998]. For a charged hole the fold fails, since "the electromagnetic field changes sign" across it, which Misner and Wheeler pointed out along with the construction [misner1957]. Charged geons exist all the same: Louko, Robert Mann, and Marolf built them in 2005 by letting the field strength change sign on a trip through the fold [louko2005].

related.text: The geon's one exterior is Schwarzschild's, metric and all, and Kruskal's full extension of it covers the geon twice. Behind the horizon the geon has a fold where Kruskal's spacetime has a second exterior [friedman1993, louko1998].
At the moment $t = 0$ the geon is Einstein and Rosen's bridge with its two sheets laid on top of each other and the opposite points of the bridge joined, as Misner and Wheeler built it [misner1957].

The same antipodal fold made on de Sitter space, where it reverses time. Made on Kruskal's spacetime with time reversed it is Gibbons's elliptic interpretation of the black hole, and the geon is the fold that keeps time's direction [gibbons1986elliptic, louko1998].
Wormhole data from Misner and Wheeler's programme of 1957. Its one hole in isotropic coordinates is the geon's moment $t = 0$ before the fold [misner1957].

Black holes of three dimensions with one exterior and a handle behind the horizon, made by identifying points of anti-de Sitter space. Their authors called them topological geons too [aminneborg1998].

coordinates.name: Kruskal

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass measured at infinity; the horizons are $X = |T|$ and the singularities $T^2 - X^2 = 1$

Areal radius, a length, the solution of $\left(r/r_s - 1\right)e^{r/r_s} = X^2 - T^2$, with $\mathrm{W}$ the principal branch of Lambert's function, $\mathrm{W}(x)\,e^{\mathrm{W}(x)} = x$; its derivatives are $\partial_T r = -2r_s^2\,T e^{-r/r_s}/r$ and $\partial_X r = 2r_s^2\,X e^{-r/r_s}/r$

coordinates.convention: We use Kruskal's coordinates $(T, X, \theta, \phi)$, with $T$ and $X$ numbers, and outside $r_s$ they are $T = \sqrt{r/r_s - 1}\,e^{r/2r_s}\sinh(ct/2r_s)$ and $X = \sqrt{r/r_s - 1}\,e^{r/2r_s}\cosh(ct/2r_s)$ for Schwarzschild's $t$ and $r$. A dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter.

coordinates.name: Schwarzschild Exterior

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass measured at infinity; both horizons lie at $r = r_s$, the future one at $t \to \infty$ and the past one at $t \to -\infty$

coordinates.convention: We use Schwarzschild's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$ on the one exterior, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $r$ the areal radius. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.

coordinates.name: Isotropic
domains: \rho = r_s/4 \;\text{(the horizons, and the throat of the moment } t = 0\text{)}

parameters.description: Schwarzschild radius, $r_s = 2GM/c^2$, with $M$ the mass measured at infinity; the throat of the moment $t = 0$ is the sphere $\rho = r_s/4$, whose areal radius is $r_s$

coordinates.convention: We use coordinates $(t, \rho, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time and $\rho$ the isotropic radius, a length, so the areal radius is $\rho(1 + r_s/4\rho)^2$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
geodesics: \ddot{\rho} + \dfrac{2048\rho^4\,r_s\left(4\rho - r_s\right)}{\left(4\rho + r_s\right)^7}\dot{t}^2 - \dfrac{2r_s}{\rho\left(4\rho + r_s\right)}\dot{\rho}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(4\rho - r_s\right)}{4\rho + r_s}\dot{\theta}^2 - \dfrac{\rho\left(4\rho - r_s\right)\sin^2\theta}{4\rho + r_s}\dot{\phi}^2 = 0
